synopsis: The class captions old photographs, and Jodi brings one of a Tokyo street corner she once lived beside. The corner half-remains and the little bakery is gone, so a single caption cannot hold it. Rose grounds the material fact; Jodi refuses to delete either tense and writes both, past and present. The learner produces the two-tense caption pair with a stated reason and a quoted thought, and the class learns that a memory can stay plural.

forbiddenClaims: surname, guessed kana name, nationality, job, or private history
age framed as frailty, confusion, or a memory-loss punchline
lived memory treated as automatic publication permission

scenes.goal: Meet Jodi through her Tokyo photo and reach the point where one caption cannot hold a place that is half-there and half-gone.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: When a place is both remembered and changed, will the class force one true caption or keep two?
scenes.learnerNeed: A two-tense captioning task where saying it was X and is now Y, with one reason, matters more than choosing a single truth.

nodes.description: A stack of old photographs goes hand to hand around the table for captioning. One stops in front of the class: a Tokyo street corner, a small shopfront on the left, the print soft at the edges. A blank caption slip waits beneath it.

nodes.intent: Drop the wistful aside about having lived in Tokyo, show the corner, and say she wants to caption this street, opening with the past.
nodes.attentionTarget: the old photo of the Tokyo street corner

nodes.resume: Jodi has decided to keep both tenses of the one corner. The learner steps in to write the two-tense caption pair for her photo, with one reason and a quoted thought.

nodes.resumeContext: The photo shows one corner that half-remains. The learner writes two captions for it — a past one (昔は、ここに小さなパン屋がありました) and a present one (今は、コンビニです) — states one reason with 〜から (匂いを覚えているから / 住んでいたから) for the ability to recall it, and reports Jodi's quoted thought with 〜と思っていた, keeping both tenses instead of choosing one.

nodes.description: The past slip and the present slip are set side by side beneath the photo. Only the tense or the reason that went missing returns for another try; the caption already written stays in place, uncrossed.

nodes.resume: Both captions now sit under the photo, each true in its own tense, with a reason attached. Jodi reads them back without erasing either.

nodes.intent: Read both captions aloud, name both as true, and make clear she is deleting neither.
nodes.attentionTarget: the two caption slips beneath the photo

nodes.description: The photo now carries two caption slips at once — one in the past tense, one in the present — pinned side by side. Neither is crossed out. The corner in the picture stays exactly as half-there as it always was.

scenes.goal: Let Jodi name why she keeps both tenses, and let the class treat plural memory as a form to master rather than a contradiction to fix.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Can two true sentences about one place count as finished, without one being made to win?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance choice about how to hold two captions of one place open at once.

nodes.resume: The learner has taken a stance on how to hold both captions open. Jodi answers by naming what the two-tense form is for.

nodes.intent: Keep both captions and place one remembered detail in the past line and one visible detail in the present line.

nodes.intent: Make a practical adjustment so both captions and the route beneath them remain readable.
nodes.attentionTarget: the caption pins and the route line beneath the photo

nodes.description: The photo is pinned to the working atlas with both captions beneath it, shifted just far enough that the route line remains visible. Bread smell belongs to the past slip; the convenience-store light belongs to the present one. Neither is crossed out.

outcomes.description: Jodi's Tokyo photo keeps two captions at once — a past-tense bakery and a present-tense convenience store — with a stated reason, and the class treats plural memory as a form to master rather than a contradiction to resolve. The corner's caption is left doubled on purpose, neither tense erased.

Jodi is introduced through her double caption: warm, unhurried, the oldest in the room and the one who studies hardest, chasing a remembered place rather than a grade. Her attention pattern — holding a remembered detail and a present detail together without forcing one to win — is established as a competence the class can lean on later.
State-ability-and-reason and past/present-comparison-with-quoted-thought evidence returns through the registered transfer activity; the story emits no lesson-completion command.

replay.withdrawnContentFallback: Use the same two-tense captioning and plural-memory beats with neutral nameplates and a generic pair who keep a past caption and a present caption for one half-changed street corner instead of choosing a single tense.
